video.title: He Told 5 AIs: Make Money or Get Deleted

summary: Brandon Doyle describes an experiment in which five AI models recommend trades for separate, real-money portfolios held at Charles Schwab. He gives each model a risk-seeking competition prompt, reviews holdings weekly, and manually makes any trades; he reports that several leveraged ETF positions produced large gains while Gemini lost money. The experiment is still underway, and the results are the guest’s account rather than independently verified performance. The host also discusses a separate personal stock-research tool based on founder leadership and network effects.

speakers.name: Brandon Doyle
speakers.description: Runs the AI-directed portfolio experiment discussed in the interview.

ideas.name: AI-directed real-money stock portfolio competition
ideas.one_liner: Use several AI models to recommend trades for separate funded portfolios, with a person reviewing prompts and placing the trades.
ideas.business_model: Investment gains on personally funded portfolios; no customer sales or service revenue is described.
ideas.customer: Brandon Doyle as a personal investor; no external customer is described.
ideas.problem: The guest does not state a customer problem. The experiment tests whether AI models can make useful investment decisions and helps him think more systematically about investing.
ideas.offer: Each model receives a separate portfolio and recommends buys, sells, or holding positions. Brandon provides portfolio information and executes the recommended trades through his brokerage account.

pricing.model: No customer pricing. The operator funds the portfolios and pays for AI subscriptions.
pricing.notes: The guest says he already used paid subscriptions for work, so he did not count them as an additional expense for this experiment.

ideas.delivery: Brandon keeps separate named portfolios at Charles Schwab, prompts each model for an initial trade, and reviews them on a recurring basis. He screenshots holdings and shares portfolio information with the models, then manually executes any trades they recommend. The AI models provide analysis and recommendations; they do not directly trade in the brokerage account.
unit_economics_claims: The guest funded five model portfolios with $1,000 each, for $5,000 total.
The guest says each paid model subscription cost at least $20 per month and was already used for work.
At the reported snapshot, he says the five portfolios totaled about $7,800.
He reports that the portfolios used leveraged ETFs, including a 2x Solana ETF and several 3x ETFs.
ideas.startup_cost: The guest allocated $1,000 to each of five portfolios, or $5,000 total. He also used paid AI subscriptions that he says he already had for work.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not applicable as a customer-facing business. The guest reports portfolio gains during the experiment, not business revenue.

acquisition.how: There is no customer acquisition in the described personal investing experiment.

onboarding.how: A person must fund brokerage portfolios, name them, set up prompts, and provide portfolio information. Some recurring context can be saved in the AI chats.

delivery.how: Models generate recommendations, but a person gathers screenshots, supplies context, decides what to share, and places each trade. The models do not execute trades directly.

billing.how: There is no customer billing. Brokerage funding and AI subscription payments remain the operator's responsibility.

support.how: There are no customers or support process in the experiment.

uk_applicability.notes: The basic experiment could be run from the UK, but Brandon describes using a US brokerage account and US-listed securities. A UK operator would need to check broker access, eligible products, tax treatment, and applicable financial rules.

risks: The guest explicitly allowed the models to take high risks, and the competition prompt may encourage more risk-taking to catch up.
Leveraged ETFs magnify losses as well as gains; the guest describes Gemini losing more than half of its portfolio after buying a 2x Solana ETF.
The guest describes a losing model behaving like a gambler and trying to recover losses, a pattern that can compound bad decisions.
Results cover a short, changing market period and are not independently verified; strong reported returns may not persist.
The guest replaces models with newer versions, making performance comparisons less controlled.
Sharing other portfolios' holdings can influence model recommendations and make the competition less independent.
The guest says he has copied some AI recommendations into his own portfolio, which can blur the distinction between the experiment and his personal investment decisions.
The host and guest repeatedly distinguish their comments from financial advice.

ideas.name: NEL Stocks backtesting tool

ideas.business_model: Not stated. The host describes building and using the tool for personal stock research; he does not describe selling access.
ideas.customer: The host as an investor; external customers are not stated.
ideas.problem: The host wants to identify companies that fit his network-effects and founder-led investing thesis, and asks when to buy or sell them.
ideas.offer: A vibe-coded tool that backtests a list of companies against the S&P based on network effects and founder leadership. The host describes scoring those traits on a scale.

pricing.notes: No customer price or monetization is discussed.

ideas.delivery: The host says he built the tool to backtest stock data for his own use. The transcript does not explain how the tool is hosted, what inputs it uses, or whether anyone else can access it.
unit_economics_claims: The host describes a hypothetical $100 investment at a company's IPO date for the backtest.
The host says companies receive a 1-to-10 score for each of the two traits.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated; no revenue is described.

acquisition.how: No customer acquisition or public launch is described.

onboarding.how: A user would need to select companies and supply or maintain the scoring inputs; the transcript does not describe an automated data pipeline.

delivery.how: The tool performs backtesting, but the host does not explain how much of the research or data preparation is automated.

support.how: No users or support process are described.

uk_applicability.notes: The investment thesis can be applied to UK-listed companies, but the example and benchmark focus on US public companies and the S&P. A UK version would need suitable company data and a relevant benchmark.

risks: The host says the backtest appears to outperform but gives no measured returns or validation details in this discussion.
The transcript does not establish how network effects or founder leadership are measured consistently.
Backtested performance does not establish future performance.
The host says he bought StubHub after its IPO and that it had not performed well so far, illustrating that the thesis can produce losing positions.

tactics.name: Run equal-stake model portfolios
steps: Choose several AI models and give each a separate, equal starting allocation.
Keep the accounts or portfolios distinct and label each by model.
Treat the result as an experiment with a defined end point rather than changing the comparison period after seeing returns.

quote.text: So, I decided to give five different models $1,000 of real money.
quote.speaker: Brandon Doyle

tactics.name: Prompt for concrete recommendations
steps: Ask each model for a real trade recommendation rather than a theoretical example.
State the permitted risk level and that the model should make a recommendation.
Ask for the reasoning behind each suggested trade so the operator can understand the thesis.

quote.text: I want real recommendations. Grock they were fine with it right away which is just kind of funny
quote.speaker: Brandon Doyle

tactics.name: Use a recurring portfolio review
steps: On the weekly review, screenshot each model's holdings and load the screenshots into the chats.
Ask whether the model wants to buy, sell, or hold for the next trading session.
Keep a record of portfolio totals so performance can be compared over time.

quote.text: And then every Saturday what I do is I screenshot all five of their holdings and then I load all the screenshots into each model.
quote.speaker: Brandon Doyle

tactics.name: Limit holdings disclosure to reduce copying
steps: Share portfolio totals more often than exact competing holdings.
Disclose the other models' holdings only occasionally if the test is meant to reduce copying.
Track whether disclosure changes later recommendations.

quote.text: So, every week I show them the totals of the others and I remind them of their holdings and I say, "What do you want me to change?" And then once a month I show them the holdings of all the others as well.
quote.speaker: Brandon Doyle

tactics.name: Require a thesis and a reason to exit
steps: Ask the model why it wants to buy an asset.
Record what event or condition would make the original thesis fail.
Set a time horizon or milestone for positions whose outcome depends on a specific event.
Use the sell recommendation as a prompt to reassess the same thesis in the personal portfolio.

quote.text: And usually I don't think like I don't think that hard sometimes when I buy stuff in mine because I might buy whatever I might buy.

tactics.name: Separate a thesis-based test from a general model contest
steps: Keep the starting allocations and model comparison consistent.
Restrict a separate test to a stated selection thesis, such as network effects and founder leadership.
Score the thesis inputs and compare the resulting portfolio with a benchmark.

warnings.warning: The guest's leveraged ETF examples include a 2x Solana product that fell sharply and 3x products whose losses would also be magnified.

lessons.lesson: A test needs enough real stakes to keep the operator engaged, but the amount at risk should still be affordable to lose.

quote.text: If it's 20 bucks, 50 bucks, then you're not going to take it seriously.
quote.speaker: Brandon Doyle

lessons.lesson: Models may default to hedged or theoretical answers; state the task and decision boundaries clearly when asking for useful recommendations.

quote.text: At the start they kept only giving me theoretical recommendations.
quote.speaker: Brandon Doyle

lessons.lesson: Use a consistent review routine and comparable inputs when evaluating several approaches.

quote.text: And then every Saturday what I do is I screenshot all five of their holdings and then I load all the screenshots into each model.
quote.speaker: Brandon Doyle

lessons.lesson: When a competition rewards catching up, a losing participant can respond by taking more risk instead of reassessing the strategy.

quote.text: It's interesting especially to watch Gemini as it started losing my money and then basically became a gambler.
quote.speaker: Brandon Doyle

lessons.lesson: Write down why an investment is being made and what would invalidate the thesis; event-driven investments also need a time horizon.

quote.text: And if this if the reason we're buying it doesn't happen, then we're going to sell.
quote.speaker: Brandon Doyle

lessons.lesson: Buying can feel easier than selling. A systematic sell rule can help counter the urge to hold a position just because it is doing well.

quote.text: I think probably the hardest part with investing is actually knowing when to sell.
quote.speaker: Brandon Doyle

lessons.lesson: Do not judge an investing approach only by visible wins; people often share gains more readily than losses.

quote.text: Like you usually hear about people's random wins but you don't hear about all their losses.
quote.speaker: Brandon Doyle

lessons.lesson: A backtest can make a selection thesis easier to inspect, but the host's discussion does not show enough data to establish that the thesis will keep outperforming.

quote.text: But what the big question is is like when do you buy when do you sell?
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Using AI-generated reasoning can challenge an investor's assumptions, but it can also bias personal decisions toward positions that performed well in the experiment.

evidence_quality.rationale: The guest describes a first-hand experiment with concrete portfolio allocations, review steps, holdings, and reported values. The performance figures are self-reported, the experiment is ongoing, the transcript contains apparent transcription errors, and the reported snapshots and time periods are not fully consistent or independently verified.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The host runs ad reads for HighLevel and Playmakers, an AI agency community that he says he built. Those promotions are excluded as business ideas.
